clue.text: Fellow, be off-you're in a pickle

parts.note: a fellow is a man
to be off is to go away

explanation.surface: Someone is told to clear off because they are in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a pickle' looks like trouble, but the definition means the fruit preserved as mango pickle or chutney.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropical fruit is a standard ingredient of Indian pickles and chutneys.

clue.text: Much ado about nothing more than a stud?

explanation.surface: A fuss over nothing, and a breeding farm.
explanation.walkthrough: A stud holds stallions; the question mark hints at a home for the females instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A fuss over an imaginary discovery; literally, a nest for female horses, beyond a stud farm.

clue.text: How unlike the Nile above Khartum

definitions.text: How unlike the Nile above Khartum

parts.words: How unlike the Nile above Khartum
parts.note: above Khartoum the Nile splits into the White and Blue Nile; a river whose name is Latin for black is unlike either

explanation.surface: A geographical comparison with the upper Nile.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word for black is also the name of a great West African river, unlike the White or Blue Nile.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin for black names a West African river, the opposite of the White and Blue Nile.

clue.text: A bird becoming so disorderly loses half its value

definitions.text: A bird becoming so disorderly loses half its value

parts.words: A bird becoming so disorderly loses half its value
parts.note: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, so one that has escaped the hand is worth half as much; the phrase also means unruly

explanation.surface: A bird that gets unruly is worth less.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush' is behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means beyond control, and literally describes a bird escaped from someone's grip.

clue.text: Fabulous coat of Wolfram ?

parts.note: the name Wolfram splits into WOLF and RAM, and the fable's wolf disguises itself in the woolly coat of a sheep

explanation.surface: A question about the coat worn by someone called Wolfram.
explanation.walkthrough: The wolf in sheep's clothing is the fable behind 'Fabulous'; Wolfram is read as wolf plus ram.
explanation.definitionFit: A wolf dressed as a ram wears a woolly hide taken from a flock animal.

clue.text: Keep sailing, say, or be for cow-keeping ?

indicators.note: say tells us the phrase is spoken and only its sound counts

parts.note: to keep sailing is to ship on

explanation.surface: Someone must choose between a life at sea and farming cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like the noun for a castle or the verb hold, but with 'sailing' it means carry on.
explanation.definitionFit: A shippon is a dialect word for a cattle shed or byre.

clue.text: How they have transformed those inn gees

definitions.text: How they have transformed those inn gees

indicators.note: transformed says the letters of inn and gees are changed into a new form

explanation.surface: Motor power has replaced the horses that once stood at inns.
explanation.walkthrough: Gees are gee-gees, horses: coaching inns lost them to the motor age, and their letters rearrange into the replacement.
explanation.definitionFit: Motors replaced coach horses at inns.

clue.text: A difficult question for one on the throne"

explanation.surface: A tough question put to a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'throne' is an artist's studio dais, where a model sits.
explanation.definitionFit: A puzzle is a tricky question; an artist's model posing sits on the studio dais.

clue.text: Warwick winning at draughts

explanation.surface: A man named Warwick is winning a board game.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, was called 'the Kingmaker' in the Wars of the Roses; in draughts a piece reaching the far row is crowned a king.
explanation.definitionFit: The earl who put kings on the English throne; in draughts, crowning a piece is a gain.

clue.text: It's north, where just a breeze is boreal -

parts.note: a breeze is a light movement of air
boreal means northern, giving another N

explanation.surface: A northern place with only a gentle wind.
explanation.walkthrough: NAIRN is a coastal town in the north of Scotland; 'where' is the definition, a place.
explanation.definitionFit: A town on the Moray Firth is a place, hence where.

clue.text: The conservatives dextrously pinioned

explanation.surface: Tory politicians have been neatly tied up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dextrously' means on the right-hand side, and 'pinioned' is having to do with a bird's wing, so the second sense is a bird's right-hand wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Conservatives form the political right; dextral means right-handed and a pinion is a wing.

clue.text: Badness best? No-hence the Commandments

parts.note: badness or wrongdoing is sin
A1 means first-class or best, with the figure 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether wickedness is best, and the answer is the Ten Commandments.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first-rate) is written AI here, the figure one standing for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Moses received the tablets of the law on the mountain of that name.

clue.text: Shoots back to the finishing line

indicators.note: back tells us the word for shoots is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to shoot a gun is to fire it, so shoots means fires

explanation.surface: Someone shoots back as they reach the end of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns FIRES round. The 'finishing line' is the small stroke that finishes off a printed letter, not a race's end.
explanation.definitionFit: In typography, the little cross-stroke finishing a letter's main stroke has this name.

clue.text: Kitchen-utensil tester who looked after the plate

parts.note: a pan is a cooking utensil
a tester is a man who tries things, a try-man

explanation.surface: A servant who tried out the cookware also cared for the silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The plate' means silver tableware, which a household servant of this kind cleaned and guarded.
explanation.definitionFit: A servant in charge of the butler's pantry kept the household silverware.

clue.text: Tell us why it's no longer a savanna

parts.note: ex- describes something that no longer is what it was
a savanna is a grassy plain

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a grassland has changed.
explanation.definitionFit: To give the reasons for something is to make it clear.

clue.text: Top gear from Atlantic to Pacific

definitions.text: Top gear from Atlantic to Pacific

parts.words: Top gear from Atlantic to Pacific
parts.note: top gear is headwear, named after the isthmus country whose canal joins the two oceans

explanation.surface: The best equipment for a voyage between oceans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top gear' looks like a car's highest gear, but means a hat; the name is that of the canal country between the two oceans.
explanation.definitionFit: A straw headpiece named after the Central American country whose canal links two oceans.

clue.text: Soothed, as one of eight who led current strikes

definitions.text: as one of eight who led current strikes

explanation.surface: An oarsman calmed his crew while setting the pace of the strokes.
explanation.walkthrough: In a rowing eight the oarsman who sets the rhythm is the stroke; to do that is to have stroked the boat. 'Current' is the water, not today.
explanation.definitionFit: Caressing gently is calming; in rowing, the pace-setting oarsman of an eight is said to stroke the crew.

clue.text: Brave Horatius had this prominence at the bridge

definitions.text: Brave Horatius had this prominence at the bridge

parts.words: Brave Horatius had this prominence at the bridge
parts.note: Horatius, the Roman who held the bridge, had a prominent nose at the bridge, where nose bridges meet the brow

explanation.surface: The Roman hero Horatius stood out when he defended the bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Macaulay's poem tells of Horatius holding the bridge; 'prominence' means a jutting nose and 'bridge' the top of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An aquiline nose with a high bridge, like those on classical statues.

clue.text: Does, to Orpheus, and Eurydice

parts.note: Dis, god of the underworld, parts Orpheus from Eurydice, so what Dis does is cut them apart

explanation.surface: An account of what happens to the mythical lovers.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as DIS SEVERS: Dis, ruler of the underworld, parts the lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: To separate or sever, read as the god Dis cutting the lovers apart.

clue.text: Island to which Helen drew those thousand ships, wrote Marlowe

definitions.text: Island to which Helen drew those thousand ships, wrote Marlowe

parts.words: Island to which Helen drew those thousand ships, wrote Marlowe
parts.note: Marlowe's Tamburlaine speaks of Helen, who drew a thousand ships to an Aegean island near Troy

explanation.surface: A literary question about Helen of Troy and the Greek fleet.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Marlowe's Tamburlaine, Part 2: Helen 'drew a thousand ships' to this island off Troy, where the Greeks hid.
explanation.definitionFit: The small Aegean isle near Troy where the Greek fleet gathered, named in Marlowe's line.

clue.text: " The —— of all Kings, Crowned and again discrowned " (L. Johnson).

definitions.text: The —— of all Kings, Crowned and again discrowned " (L. Johnson

parts.words: The —— of all Kings, Crowned and again discrowned " (L. Johnson
parts.note: the gap completes Lionel Johnson's line on Charles I, calling him the most sorrowful of kings

explanation.surface: A quotation from Lionel Johnson's poem on the statue of King Charles I.
explanation.walkthrough: Lionel Johnson's 'By the Statue of King Charles at Charing Cross' calls Charles I the most sorrowful of kings.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of unhappy fills the gap in Johnson's line about the executed king.

clue.text: Sounds funny to be up in arms

indicators.note: sounds says the word for funny is heard rather than seen

parts.note: funny means comic or amusing

explanation.surface: Something that seems funny turns out to cause outrage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up in arms' looks like anger, but it means located in the upper arm.
explanation.definitionFit: The long bone of the upper limb runs from shoulder to elbow.

clue.text: One who kept cocks on his heath?

definitions.text: One who kept cocks on his heath?

parts.words: One who kept cocks on his heath?
parts.note: the cocks are heaps of dried grass, not birds, and the parish officer in charge of fences and commons looked after them

explanation.surface: A man who raised cockerels on his moorland.
explanation.walkthrough: A hayward was a manor officer guarding fences and common land; the 'cocks' are haycocks, piles of dried grass.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval parish officer in charge of hedges and commons, read as a guard of haycocks.

clue.text: What we pass with a friend that is on the watch

definitions.text: What we pass with a friend

explanation.surface: Friends chat while one keeps a lookout.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'pass the time of day' is to exchange greetings; a watch shows the hour, and 'on the watch' sounds like keeping guard.
explanation.definitionFit: Exchanging pleasantries is passing it with someone; a clock face shows the current hour.

clue.text: One of them was an early motorist-but these tools were not in the kit

definitions.text: One of them was an early motorist-but these tools were not in the kit

parts.words: One of them was an early motorist-but these tools were not in the kit
parts.note: Mr Toad of The Wind in the Willows was a reckless early driver, and the plural plus tools makes a fungus, not a spanner

explanation.surface: An early motorist's tool kit lacked some items.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Toad in Kenneth Grahame's 'The Wind in the Willows' is a car-mad driver; adding 'tools' to the answer gives toadstools, which no kit holds.
explanation.definitionFit: The warty amphibians, one of whom was Grahame's motoring Mr Toad.

clue.text: Prize for Genevieve ?

parts.note: Genevieve is the 1953 British film about a vintage car, and a film may win an Academy Award

explanation.surface: A prize for a woman named Genevieve.
explanation.walkthrough: Genevieve was a 1953 British comedy about a veteran car rally, nominated for Academy Awards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuette is the film world's top prize.

clue.text: Serve ill or take to arms

explanation.surface: Someone either does a bad job or heads off to fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serve ill' looks like 'serve badly' but means serve the sick; 'take to arms' means cradle, not go to war.
explanation.definitionFit: A carer tends the sick; one may also cradle a baby in one's arms.

clue.text: Come to and-stretch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Come to' looks like waking up, but means arrive at.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrive at a place; and to extend an arm out.

clue.text: Ha, cod: pie for " a special case"

indicators.note: printer's pie is type that has been jumbled up, so pie signals the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Someone laughs at a fish pie made for one occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pie' is the printer's term for spilt, jumbled type, so HA and COD are mixed up.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means made for one particular purpose only.

clue.text: East-end socialist to speechify in great detail

parts.note: the end of the word East that starts it is E, also the compass abbreviation
Lab is short for Labour, the British socialist party
to speechify is to orate

explanation.surface: A left-wing politician from London's East End gives a long-winded speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is a district of London, but here it supplies just E. Lab is the abbreviation for the Labour Party, Britain's socialist party.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worked out with much intricate care is highly detailed.

clue.text: Steep result maybe

parts.note: to steep is to soak, and something left to soak ends up soaked through

explanation.surface: A sharp outcome, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steep' looks like a sharp rise, but it is the verb meaning soak.
explanation.definitionFit: Soaking something thoroughly leaves it wholly filled with liquid.

clue.text: What's so moral in scarlet hose?

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words scarlet hose

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what is so virtuous about red stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: The moral character or guiding spirit of a group or person.
